extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate geoscience students and instructors (those learning or teaching hypothesis testing and proposal writing in geoscience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for undergraduate students on applying the geoscientific method and hypothesis-testing approaches when framing research questions and writing geoscience proposals. Emphasizes historical and contemporary methodological perspectives useful for students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple working hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the method of multiple working hypotheses (as articulated by G. K. Gilbert and T. C. Chamberlin) rather than prematurely committing to a single explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical papers by Gilbert (1886) and Chamberlin (1897) fully articulate and explore this method; they remain inspirational reading for students. Using multiple hypotheses helps frame research in a way that avoids bias and supports comparative testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply rigorous scientific thinking (linear hypothesis-testing where appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow a recipe for rigorous scientific thinking and linear hypothesis testing when appropriate to the question and examples at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson (1933) presents a detailed articulation of linear hypothesis testing using geologic examples; this classical approach can help undergraduates structure hypothesis-driven inquiry and proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and manage non-linear interpretation in geosciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that interpretation and reasoning in the geosciences are often fundamentally non-linear, and incorporate methods that reflect that complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frodeman (1995) argues for the non-linear nature of geoscientific interpretation; students should be aware that data interpretation may require iterative, non-linear reasoning rather than a strictly linear test-confirm model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek decisive ('smoking gun') evidence to validate hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, design studies and proposals to identify clear, decisive evidence that can validate or falsify competing hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleland (2001) describes a 'smoking gun' approach to validating hypotheses; proposals should aim to specify observations or analyses that would provide strong discriminatory power among hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame, articulate, and tackle research questions using geoscientific method principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a shared understanding of the geoscientific method to articulate, frame, and tackle research questions in proposals and student research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The geoscientific method comprises how geoscientists articulate and frame questions and choose methods to address them; students should explicitly state research questions, justify their framing, and align methods to hypothesis-testing goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accessible, exemplary literature to learn methods and proposal conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement limited undergraduate textbook coverage with accessible papers and essays that exemplify geoscientific hypothesis testing and proposal-writing conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summary notes that most undergraduate texts provide a paltry introduction; students should read selected seminal and recent papers (e.g., Gilbert, Chamberlin, Johnson, Frodeman, Cleland) that are accessible and provide models for reasoning and proposal structure.
